catholic-encyclopedia-1913-modena: Modena, the Emilian city of the Este dukes, has been an archbishop's see since the early Church. This entry covers its cathedral, its bishops, and its history. The faith in the land of balsamic and engines, where the Este dukes built churches and palaces.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-modigliana: Modigliana, the Tuscan hill town of the Guidi counts, became a bishop's see in the 1800s. This entry covers its diocese, its churches, and its history. A young diocese in an old town, carved from the ancient see of Faenza.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-montana: Montana's Catholic story runs from the Jesuit missions to the Flathead to the dioceses of Helena and Great Falls. This entry covers its bishops, parishes, and the Church's growth in Big Sky country. The faith in the last best place.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-myrina: Myrina was a city of ancient Aeolis on the Aegean coast, and its early bishopric survives only as a titular see. This brief entry notes its site and its church history. A quiet name from the ancient map, its bishops recorded in the old lists.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-north-carolin: North Carolina's Catholic story runs from the first missions to the dioceses of Raleigh and Charlotte. This entry covers its bishops, parishes, and institutions. The faith in the Tar Heel State: its cathedral at Raleigh serves a growing flock to this day.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-novena: A novena is nine days of prayer for a special intention, from the apostles' nine days between Ascension and Pentecost. This entry explains its origin, its forms, and its indulgences. Nine days of asking: its novenas honor saints from Christmas to Pentecost.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-nueva-pamplon: Nueva Pamplona, the Colombian city of the Andes, became an archdiocese serving the country's northeast. This entry covers its bishops, churches, and history. The faith in the high cordillera: its cathedral serves the Andean northeast of Colombia to this day.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-oppido-mamert: Oppido Mamertina, the Calabrian town of the Aspromonte, has been a bishop's see since Norman times. This entry covers its diocese, its churches, and its history. The faith in the toe's interior: its bishops served the Aspromonte mountain towns for centuries.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-orcagna: Orcagna was the Florentine master whose tabernacle at Orsanmichele is a wonder of Gothic art. This entry covers his career, his works in painting and sculpture, and his fame. Florence's architect of the beautiful: his tabernacle took nine years to carve.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-palestrina: Palestrina was both the ancient town and Giovanni Pierluigi, the prince of church music whose Masses saved polyphony. This entry covers the town, the composer, and his immortal music. The city and the master: his Missa Papae Marcelli is immortal.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pamplona: Pamplona, the Navarrese capital of the running of the bulls, has been a bishop's see since the early Church. This entry covers its diocese, its bishops, and its history. The faith in the city of San Fermín: its cathedral guards Navarre's old faith.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-parana: Paraná, the Brazilian state of the great plains, built its Catholic life around the archdiocese of Curitiba. This entry covers its dioceses, bishops, and history. The faith in the land of the pines: its noble cathedral proudly crowns the growing city of Curitiba.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pedro-campana: Pedro Campaña was the Flemish-born painter whose altarpieces adorned Seville's churches. This entry sketches his career, his works, and his place. The Fleming of Andalusia: his great Descent from the Cross still hangs in Seville's grand old Gothic cathedral today.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pedro-de-luna: Pedro de Luna was Benedict XIII, the stubborn antipope who held Avignon against councils and kings. This entry traces his long schism, his deposition, and his lonely death. The pope who would not yield: his Peñíscola became the last papal court.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-peter-blomeve: This biographical entry profiles Peter Blomevenna, a Carthusian prior of the 1500s, tracing his career, his writings, and his place as the 1913 editors recorded it. A compact life from the encyclopedia's Carthusian gallery, preserved among its records of Cologne priors.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-piazza-armeri: Piazza Armerina, the Sicilian town of the great Roman villa, became a diocese. This entry covers its bishops, churches, and history. The Church among the mosaics of Casale: its proud old cathedral still crowns the ancient Sicilian hill town today.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pietro-alagon: Pietro Alagona was the Jesuit theologian whose compendium of Suarez trained the schools. This entry covers his career, his works, and his influence. The abbreviator of the great doctor: his handy compendium long served the Jesuit seminaries of all Europe.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-piscina: The piscina is the church's sacred basin for the ablutions of the Mass. This entry explains its form, its placement, and its ritual use. The little well of the sanctuary: its small drain returns the holy waters to consecrated earth.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-poona: Poona became the diocese of western India's Catholics. This entry covers its bishops, churches, and institutions as of 1913. The faith in the Deccan's garden city: its noble cathedral serves the vast Maratha country all around it in living faith.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-porto-and-san: Porto and Santa Rufina is the suburbicarian see of the cardinal dean's tradition. This entry covers its bishops, its antiquity, and its churches. The ancient see at Rome's gate: its ancient cardinal ranks first among all the bishops of the Church.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-rajpootana: Rajpootana was the mission of Rajasthan's princely states. This entry covers its stations, its missionaries, and its work as of 1913. The faith in the land of kings: its humble chapels dot the Thar desert of India's far west in faith.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ratherius-of-: Ratherius of Verona was the bishop-scholar of the tenth century. This entry notes his writings, his exiles, and his erudition. The learned exile of Lotharingia: his bitter satires lashed the corrupt clergy of Verona's dark age in verse and prose.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ravenna: Ravenna became the archdiocese of the exarchate's capital. This entry covers its archbishops, its mosaics, and its history. The city of the golden apses: its ancient mosaics glow in the Byzantine churches of Ravenna's old center in gold and blue.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-regina: Regina became the archdiocese of Saskatchewan's capital. This entry covers its archbishops, churches, and institutions as of 1913. The faith on the prairie: its new cathedral serves the prairie capital of Regina in living faith today still shining bright and true.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-remesiana: Remesiana, the Dacian town of the Balkan passes, once had a Christian bishop. This brief entry notes its site and its early church history. A quiet name from Moesia: its ancient bishop signed the councils of old in the fourth age.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-rhesaena: Rhesaena, the Mesopotamian town of the upper Khabur, once had a Christian bishop. This brief entry notes its site and its early church history. A quiet name from Osrhoene: its old stones remember the bishop of old in the desert.

dutt-mahabharata-shanti-anushasana:
Dutt joined the Shanti and Anushasana Parvas in one English volume in 1908. The Mahabharata's two great books of teaching stand together here. Bhishma on his arrow-bed speaks the epic's whole moral system.

farina:
George Meredith's Farina is an early tale in prose and verse set in medieval Cologne. Rich Gottlieb Groschen, the Kaiser's money-lender, rules the city's trade from his fig-tree's shade. His daughter Margarita is the White Rose of Germany. Young men of the White Rose Club break heads daily in her honour.

farmers-of-forty-centuries-or-permanent-:
F. H. King's Farmers of Forty Centuries, published in 1911 with a preface by L. H. Bailey, reports permanent agriculture in China, Korea, and Japan. King, a soil physicist, travelled to see how the East had farmed the same fields for four thousand years. Bailey's preface states the lesson: farming stands or falls on keeping the soil fertile. The oriental peoples solved it.

Chapters survey canal digging, surface fitting of fields, and the fuel problem. The utilization of waste in Shantung shows every scrap returned to the soil. Rice culture, silk culture, and the tea industry receive full treatment. King measured densities Western farmers found incredible: crowds of people fed from tiny, manured plots. His book founded a Western tradition of organic and sustainable farming. It still reads as fieldwork, not theory, from a scientist who went to learn.

Daily life, pride, and tender feeling pull the lovers in opposed ways. Gjellerup blends thought and feeling, asking what love owes to truth. The prose is quiet rather than showy, and the pain feels earned. Readers who know only his Indian novel will find a gentler, nearer Gjellerup here, writing of his own land and people.

juana:
Juana, also called The Maranas, is a story by Honoré de Balzac, translated by Katharine Prescott Wormeley. Balzac dedicates it to Madame la Comtesse Merlin. The opening chapter is named Exposition. It begins with the taking of Tarragona by Marshal Suchet's army in Spain.

Discipline failed for a short spell after the victory, and the sack looked much like pillage. Suchet restored order, appointed a commandant, and set French administration running. Yet Spaniards kept their own ways in private, giving the city a mongrel aspect. One Italian regiment, full of troublesome sons of good families, stands out in Balzac's account. From this occupation world, his tale of Juana and the Marana family grows.

nasa-tm-19660013086-static-longitudinal-:

The shape was a V/STOL design, meant to take off and land vertically or in short distances. Two wing ideas were tried on it. One wing swept its outer panels back seventy-five degrees. The other was a skewed wing, turned at angles up to ninety degrees.

Pitching moment changed in a straight line with lift for both layouts, at modest settings. Raising the skew angle changed that behavior step by step. Such bold wings promised one aircraft for both slow lift and fast flight. Tunnel data at high speed was the first check on whether the promise could hold.

It investigates how liquid propellant moves inside a large rocket booster. Loose liquid sloshing in a tank can disturb a vehicle's flight, so its motion matters.

The authors present experimental data on liquid hydrogen in the wide tank of an S-IVB stage. The data cover the boost phase, the moment of stage cutoff, and time in orbit. During boost, they report, the height of the sloshing liquid fell as the flight went on. Such records help designers predict and calm slosh.
nasa-tm-19680017989-vacuum-hot-pressing-:
Donald R. Rummler of Langley Research Center studied vacuum hot pressing of magnesium aluminate in this paper, presented in October 1966. Magnesium aluminate, also called spinel, is a ceramic oxide powder. Hot pressing squeezes the powder at high heat until it becomes a dense solid.

Rummler tested whether a proposed rate equation could describe the pressing process. He tracked densification across a wide range of temperatures and pressures. Below the top range, the material behaved much like other oxide systems. Above it, neither standard creep nor plastic flow models fit the observed behavior. The rate equation, treating porosity as its own variable, described the results well overall.
nasa-tm-19680027027-radar-scatterometer-:
Radar Scatterometer Data Validation is the final report of the Flight Research Projects Branch at the Manned Spacecraft Center in Houston. Dated March 29, 1968, and numbered MSC-CA-R-68-1, it checks data from a radar scatterometer. That instrument measures how strongly the ground or sea reflects radar signals at slanting angles, a clue to surface type and wind.

Chapters move from theory to the validation test procedure, then to results and discussion. Tables give rolloff functions for missions over land and over water, plus antenna pattern factors. Appendices supply reference data for many terrain types and samples of scatterometer data. Figures trace how radar return changes with wind speed over the sea.
nasa-tm-19690012889-tos-evaluation-cente:
Robert R. Golden of Goddard Space Flight Center, with Duane A. Kaeding and David E. Briggs of RCA Service Company, report TOS Evaluation Center test results for ESSA 4. Their paper, X-481-69-37, is dated January 1969. ESSA 4 was a working weather satellite, and the center tested how its command, control, and working systems had degraded in service.

The tests fall into three groups, each run under stated purpose, procedure, and results headings. Group one covers spacecraft receiver degradation after operations. It also covers pictures taken while the spacecraft sat in darkness. A third test probes how vulnerable the command system is to false or stray signals. Later groups extend the checking across further subsystems of the satellite.
nasa-tm-19700025402-csm-rendezvous-proce:
Command and service module rendezvous procedures for the G mission fill this Houston final report, number MSC-CF-P-69-11. The G mission was Apollo 11, the first landing flight. If the lunar module could not complete its own rendezvous, the command module would have to fly down and fetch the crew.

The report lays out rules, detailed step-by-step procedures for the normal mission, and a summary of command module attitudes. A long later section describes fifteen abort and rescue cases, one by one. Each case carries a one-page onboard rescue checklist, a relative motion plot, and a pad page. The cases run from partial descent burns to missed powered descent starts.
nasa-tm-19710007848-prejud-a-computer-co:
Thor T. Semler of the Lewis Research Center wrote this report on a computer code named PREJUD. The code gives a first analysis of data from two-dimensional pulse height analyzers. Such instruments count radiation events by their energy and kind.

PREJUD sorts gamma ray counts apart from neutron counts on its own. It then puts the results into a form that spectrum codes can accept. Semler details the strategy used for that separation. He also describes the smoothing methods and the curve fitting the code applies. Clean sorting at this first stage decides how much the later analysis can be trusted.
notable-women-of-modern-china:
Margaret E. Burton published Notable Women of Modern China with Fleming H. Revell in 1912. Burton had written The Education of Women in China before it. A picture shows Dr Hü King Eng at her graduation from medical college. The book costs a dollar and a quarter in the publisher's list.

That list calls the lives striking biographies, and Burton able to treat them with interest and discernment. If such women are types for a great company to follow, it says, a nation's future is assured. Her earlier book was called thrilling and revealing by the Christian Advocate. Chinese women in medicine and study stand at the centre here.
plotinus-enneads-mackenna:
Plotinus, the founder of Neoplatonism, wrote the treatises of the Enneads in the third century AD; his pupil Porphyry arranged them after his death. Stephen MacKenna's English translation, made between 1917 and 1930, is praised as a work of art in itself. The text here follows that version in five volumes.

Plotinus teaches that all things flow from the One, a source beyond being and thought. Soul descends into body and can climb back by beauty, thought, and contemplation. The 54 treatises treat the soul, the stars, providence, beauty, and the mystic union with the One. His system shaped Christian, Jewish, and Muslim theology for a thousand years.
podcast-joerogan-R9x8betNlNA:
Nature and ancient ruins humble the host in this reflective Joe Rogan Experience segment. Rogan talks about how wild places and the remains of old civilizations cut people down to size. Awe, he argues, is the proper response to deep time and raw nature.

The talk moves from forests and oceans to the stones of peoples long vanished. Rogan and his guest weigh how short a human life is against mountains and empires of dust. They ask what such humility does to a person's pride and plans. Humble and awestruck listeners get the host pondering deep time in a quieter register.
podcast-tuckercarlson-3XgusCSBtNA:
Tucker Carlson hosts debate night from Bedminster, Donald Trump's New Jersey club. Guests and friends gather to watch the candidates clash on screen. The host gives his crowd a ringside role.

Reactions come live as lines land and gaffes pile up. Carlson scores the night for viewers who trust his read. The setting adds wealth, loyalty, and spectacle to the show. The episode works as both watch party and instant analysis. It captures how a campaign night feels inside the winner's circle, among people sure of the outcome they want.
podcast-tuckercarlson-JaKuo6w9TnA:
Official stories about 9/11, the Kennedy assassination, and Gaza come under attack in this Tucker Carlson episode. Carlson argues that lies about these events serve the same goal: pushing America toward wider war, even nuclear war. The survey is dark by design, linking decades of deception.

Carlson moves case by case through the claims he says do not hold up. He asks who gains when the public accepts a false story and stops asking questions. The episode ends on his warning about escalation with Iran and Russia. Questioning viewers get the host's full charge against the war machine.
podcast-tuckercarlson-rFgLe03bVnA:
Tucker Carlson reports on how Christians are treated in the Holy Land by an Israel backed by US funds. The episode title calls the truth of it shocking. Carlson builds the report from tales on the ground.

Carlson shares cases of blocked worship, seized land, and fear among old Christian towns. He argues US cash props up the state that lets it stand. He asks why US churches stay so quiet. Listeners get a report that cuts against the grain of most US press. The library keeps the episode as a record of his stated case.
pollyanna:
Eleanor H. Porter created the most famous optimist in American fiction in Pollyanna, the story of an orphan sent to live with her stern Aunt Polly in a Vermont town. The contents lay out the machinery: Miss Polly, old Tom and Nancy, the coming of Pollyanna, the little attic room, and then the chapter simply called the Game. The game is the glad game, taught by her minister father: find something to be glad about in everything, even a pair of crutches.

Pollyanna plays it on the whole town, on the bedridden Mrs. Snow, the recluse John Pendleton, and the orphan Jimmy Bean, until an accident stops her own legs and the town must play it back to her. Porter's novel, dedicated to her cousin Belle, named an attitude for the language itself. Sentimental, engineered, and utterly effective, the book still defines the word it invented.
ramona:
Ramona, by Helen Hunt Jackson, opens at sheep-shearing time in Southern California. The scene is the ranch of the Señora Moreno. The shearing is late because her eldest son Felipe has been ill. Since his father's death Felipe has stood at the head of the house, and nothing, the Señora holds, can be done without him.

In truth, the narrator says, it is the Señora, Gonzaga Moreno, who decides everything from the sheep-pastures to the artichoke-patch, though only she knows it. Quiet and reserved, with rosary in hand, she veils an imperious, passionate nature. That nature had been tossed by the Bay of Biscay, the Gulf of Mexico, and the Pacific.
religions-of-ancient-china:
Herbert A. Giles, professor of Chinese at Cambridge, wrote this short survey for the series Religions: Ancient and Modern. Constable of London first published it in 1906. A preparer's note lists its companion volumes, on subjects from Judaism and Shinto to ancient Egypt and Islam.

Chapter one, The Ancient Faith, opens with a striking claim about Chinese thought. The problem of the universe, Giles says, never offered the slightest difficulty to Chinese philosophers. His survey then sets out their theory of how the world is ordered. Giles had also written Historic China and a history of Chinese literature, and he writes here for general readers.
strange-true-stories-of-louisiana:
George W. Cable, author of The Grandissimes and Bonaventure, published Strange True Stories of Louisiana in 1890, with illustrations. A first chapter explains how he got the tales, which he presents as true accounts drawn from old papers and memories of the state.

The contents open with The Young Aunt with White Hair. They then follow Francoise and Suzanne on an expedition down Bayou Plaquemine. Storms, robbers, and a ball follow. Partings in a place called Little Paris close their tale. Alix de Morainville gets her own section, and a life of Salome Muller, called the white slave, follows. Creole Louisiana, with its mix of French grace and hard history, fills the book.
the-awakening-of-china:
W. A. P. Martin, once president of the Chinese Imperial University, wrote a survey of China in two large parts. Martin is also named for A Cycle of Cathay and The Siege in Peking. Part one, called the empire in outline, tours China Proper province by province.

Chapters move from Kwangtung and Fukien through the river provinces to the north-west and outlying lands such as Manchuria, Mongolia, Turkestan, and Tibet. Part two gives history in outline, from early origins and a mythical period through the Three Dynasties and the house of Chou. Sages, warring states, and later dynasties carry the account toward the eighteenth century.
the-chinese-classics-prolegomena: James Legge's prolegomena to The Chinese Classics is named here as the second item in a series of his works, but only the Project Gutenberg header is present. That header carries the standard copyright warnings and notes on keeping the file for later readers.Its contents rest on the strength of the title page alone.
the-civilization-of-china:
Herbert A. Giles, Professor of Chinese at Cambridge and once a British consul at Ningpo, wrote this outline of Chinese civilization. His preface, dated Cambridge, May 12, 1911, sets a modest aim. The book sketches that civilization from the earliest times down to a present period of rapid and startling transition.

Giles wrote first for readers who know little or nothing of China, hoping to draw them toward a wider, more ordered survey. Chapter I, The Feudal Age, starts with a plain question: what does the term China mean? In its widest sense it covers Mongolia, Manchuria, Eastern Turkestan, Tibet, and the Eighteen Provinces. That whole spans some five million square miles, more than twice the size of the United States. For manners, customs, and thought, though, he narrows the field to the Chinese heartland.
the-commonwealth-of-oceana:
James Harrington's Oceana sets out his design for an ideal commonwealth, and a long introduction here gives his life first. Harrington, eldest son of Sir Sapcotes Harrington of Exton in Rutlandshire, was born in January 1611, in the reign of James I. He came five years before Shakespeare's death and was two or three years younger than John Milton.

His great-grandfather, Sir James Harrington, married Lucy, daughter of Sir William Sidney, and lived with her to their golden wedding day. Through eighteen children he counted himself, before his death, patriarch of a vast kindred. That family produced dukes, marquises, earls, viscounts, and barons by the dozen, sixteen of them Knights of the Garter. The introduction stresses the point: Oceana's designer stood close to England's chief nobility. As a child Harrington was studious and unusually sedate.
the-fight-for-the-republic-in-china: Only the old Project Gutenberg header is present here, before the book itself begins. It names The Fight for the Republic in China by B. L. Putnam Weale, and gives the book's release data. No title page, contents list, or chapter text is included in this portion, so nothing about the author's account of China can be judged from the front pages alone.
the-first-discovery-of-australia-and-new:
George Collingridge wrote this account of the first finding of Australia and New Guinea, first printed in 1906. He draws on the tales of Portuguese and Spanish voyages between 1492 and 1606 and on their old charts.

The contents run from the hunt for the Spice Islands to maps by Ribero, Desceliers, and Desliens that show a great south land. Chapters take up Villalobos, Mendana's finds in the Solomons, Queiroz, and Torres. Pictures of Prince Henry, Magellan, and old ships fill the front. Collingridge argues that Iberian sailors charted these coasts long before the Dutch or English came.
the-gentleman-from-indiana:
Booth Tarkington wrote The Gentleman from Indiana as a novel of a young editor in a flat-land Indiana town. John Harkless stands at the center from the first chapter.

Tarkington opens on the level fields of Indiana, bleak with mud and snow in winter and hot and dusty in summer, where small frame stations stand far apart. Into such a town comes Harkless to run a paper and stay. Chapters bring a strange lady, a court-house bell, a rescue, and a treachery by a man named Fisbee. Tarkington draws small-town pride, rough politics, and a young man's fight to be both firm and kind.
the-girl-from-montana: Grace Livingston Hill wrote The Girl from Montana. Grosset and Dunlap printed it in New York, dated 1922. Only front matter is present here. It gives the title page and a long list of other books by Hill. That list names April Gold and The Beloved Stranger. It names The Honor Girl, Kerry, Marigold, and Crimson Roses. It also names The Mystery of Mary and A Girl to Come Home To. No chapter text is present. Nothing about the plot of this novel can be told from what is here.
the-naval-war-of-1812-or-the-history-of-:
Theodore Roosevelt's The Naval War of 1812 is present here only in front matter from a later edition, so Roosevelt's history itself does not appear. The full title adds an account of the Battle of New Orleans. An introduction by Edward K. Eckert is announced on the title page, though its text is not among the pages shown.

What the pages do show is a list of illustrations. Captain Isaac Hull and three views of the Constitution fighting the Guerriere open it. The Wasp against the Frolic, Captains Decatur, Bainbridge, and Lawrence, the Chesapeake against the Shannon, the Battle of Lake Erie, and the Essex follow. A contents list promises only illustrations and an index by name.
the-pioneers-or-the-sources-of-the-susqu:
J. Fenimore Cooper's The Pioneers, or The Sources of the Susquehanna, is introduced as a descriptive tale. Cooper warns that he mixed literal fact with a general picture of the country. Scenes and characters familiar from his own youth tempted him toward what he had known. He might otherwise have imagined more freely. The county, he notes, can only be Otsego, and the lake only the source of the Susquehanna.

His short history of the district follows Otsego from its days inside Albany County, through Montgomery, to county status shortly after the peace of 1783. The lake sits among low spurs of the Alleghanies, on some of the highest land in New York. Settlers' manners, the face of the country, and its climate are all described from the author's own recollections. He offers those memories as his apology for their detail.
the-problem-of-china: Bertrand Russell's The Problem of China was first published in 1922; the copy described is a 1966 second impression. Its epigraph retells Chuang Tze's parable of Chaos, whose well-meaning friends bored him seven orifices and killed him. Chapter I, Questions, begins with a receptive European newly arrived in China facing puzzling questions. Only the title pages, epigraph, and the chapter's first lines are present in the pages at hand, so Russell's argument is not yet under way.
the-tragedy-of-st-helena:
Sir Walter Runciman's Tragedy of St. Helena, published by T. Fisher Unwin in 1911, opens with a sailors' song: 'Oh! Boney was ill-treated.' Runciman, a seaman himself, once held anti-Napoleonic ideas, yet the chant impressed him. Years later, on a bookstall before a long voyage, he bought Scott's Life of Napoleon meaning to have his opinion confirmed. Careful reading convinced him instead that Boney was ill-treated, and that Scott had collected evidence to exonerate the English government.

That reversal launched Runciman's own study of Napoleon's exile. He writes as a sailor judging landsmen's treatment of a prisoner, with sympathy from forecastle songs. Readers interested in the St. Helena controversy get an unusual witness: a merchant seaman turned baronet arguing that England shamed itself over its captive emperor.
the-two-gentlemen-of-verona: Shakespeare's Two Gentlemen of Verona is named by this record, but the pages present again carry Michael S. Hart's general editor's note on old printing errors, the same note found before several other plays in this set. It explains cliches of type, exchanged u and v, and scholars' reverence for the old spellings. The note closes by presenting 'the first Part of Henry the Sixt,' which is not this play at all, a plain mismatch. No Valentine, Proteus, or line of the comedy appears in what is shown.
their-mariposa-legend-a-romance-of-santa:
Charlotte Herr opens Their Mariposa Legend, a romance of Santa Catalina, in a mythic island spring. She dedicates the book to little Bruce Parker, who loved stories. Centuries ago, rain brought spring to Punagwandah, fairest of the Channel Islands. Lilac bloomed on steep hillsides above a radiant sea. Larks sang while lilies filled shadowed canyon niches with light. Princess Wildenai watched the dawn from her cavern bower.

Wildenai was the sweetest blossom of that spring, Herr writes. She was loveliest among the Mariposa maidens and of royal blood. Chief Torquam, sleeping below on the beach, knew more of her birth than he told. Legend, romance, and California island scenery blend here. Herr also wrote The Wise Mamma Goose for children.
tomlinsoniana:
Edward Bulwer-Lytton presents the posthumous writings of Augustus Tomlinson, celebrated professor of moral philosophy at an unnamed university. The writings comprise maxims on creating, illustrated by ten characters, and a second part of critical, sentimental, and moral essays called Brachylogia. An introduction recounts the editor's German travels.

At Tomlinson's university he learned the professor died in early 1822 after a lingering illness, still discussing ethical philosophy on his deathbed. Pupils recalled his green silk dressing-gown, black velvet cap, and pepper-and-salt small-clothes. Readers get satirical moral essays wrapped in a fond, gossipy memoir of their supposed author.
true-love-s-reward-a-sequel-to-mona:
Mrs. Georgie Sheldon's True Love's Reward, printed in 1891, continues her novel Mona. Sheldon also wrote Virgie's Inheritance, Trixy, and Helen's Victory. Chapter one is headed A New Discovery Deepens a Mystery.

Mrs. Montague comes to her room an hour after Mona went upstairs, frowning deeply. Mona waits in a white wrapper, ready to help her undress, and takes off the rich dress and jewels with patient care. The lady answers her courtesy with curt monosyllables. They will return to New York on the eleven o'clock express, and Mona must mend a traveling suit before nine. The sequel opens on strained manners and a hidden grievance.
universite-de-paris-faculte-de-theologie: Paris printers issued this censure by the Faculty of Theology of the University of Paris in 1784. Its title pages, in Latin and French, name the target: Principes de Morale, a book by the Abbe de Mably. The faculty's formal finding against that book is the work's whole subject. The printer Alexandre Jombert the younger sold it on the rue Dauphine, with royal approval. The pages present here are the Latin and French title pages only, in rough old type. The censure text itself is not shown.
with-moore-at-corunna: Only the title page and contents are present here for G. A. Henty's With Moore at Corunna, so the tale itself does not appear. Wal Paget drew twelve pictures for the book. The contents open with the Mayo Fusiliers and two dangers. Landings, canvas camps, and the battles of Rolica and Vimiera follow. A pause, an advance, and a false alarm build toward the retreat. Corunna itself comes at chapter ten. An escape and a dangerous mission close the part shown.
zanetto-and-cavalleria-rusticana:
Pietro Mascagni composed these two short operas, with libretti by G. Targioni-Tozzetti and G. Menasci. Willard G. Day rendered the words into English for this souvenir libretto. The Zanetto plot summary opens the volume. Silvia, a rich and lovely hotel keeper, has refused every suitor. None stirred her heart, so she has sworn off love for good. Yet she remembers a youth she once saw near Florence.

That memory sets the one-act tale moving toward a meeting. Cavalleria Rusticana, the far more famous companion piece, shares the bill. Theatregoers got both plots and texts in one cheap booklet. Readers can follow sung drama in English print.
